original_question: Is there a finitely presented orderable group with insoluble word problem?
target_in_paper: Section 3 ("Totally ordered groups"), Problem 3.29*: "Is there a finitely presented orderable group with insoluble word problem?"; the paper explicitly flags it as the orderable analogue of Problem 2.22 for right-orderable groups. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.2621.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's official problem almost word for word and gets the three essential ingredients exactly right: finite presentability, orderability (not merely right-orderability), and insolubility of the word problem. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.2621.pdf))
missing_details: To make it fully stand-alone, "orderable" should be unpacked in the paper's Section 3 sense: the group must admit a total order making it a totally ordered group, i.e. compatible with left as well as right multiplication, not just a right order. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.2621.pdf))

It is helpful to say explicitly that the group is finitely presented in the ordinary group-theoretic language; in this paper, when an expanded language is intended, the authors say so explicitly, as in Problem 1.43 for ℓ-groups. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.2621.pdf))

For self-containment, you may wish to specify that "word problem" is meant in the usual group-theoretic sense for the finitely presented group. The paper itself states the problem without further elaboration here. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.2621.pdf))

The paper's "cf. Problem 2.22" matters: the nearby right-orderable analogue is distinct and is recorded in the paper as already solved positively, so the refined question must stay specifically about two-sided orderability. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.2621.pdf))
refined_question: Does there exist a finitely presented group G that is orderable, in the sense that G admits a total order invariant under both left and right multiplication, and whose group-theoretic word problem is insoluble?
justification: The draft targets Problem 3.29*, not the solved right-orderable Problem 2.22, because the key word is "orderable." Section 3 sets the ambient class to ordered/orderable groups, viewed as the two-sided analogue of the right-ordered setting, and Problem 3.29 then asks this question verbatim. The only nearby extra information is Comment 3.29, which gives a one-way consequence (about maximal elements in the lattice of quasi-varieties of orderable groups), not an equivalence. So the sharpest paper-faithful rewrite is to keep the question unchanged in scope while unpacking the meaning of orderability and the presentation context. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0906.2621.pdf))
